title: App Flow Reader
user: Knowledge workers with progressive low vision who must complete recurring tasks in dense web applications such as Salesforce, PowerBI, and internal tools.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A knowledge worker losing vision reports that voice control and keyboard shortcuts break down in modern browser apps without keybindings.
The open issue is titled 'Windows: Screen reader accessibility missing completely,' showing that even a developer tool can leave a navigation gap.

recurrence: Two independent 2025 requests identify inaccessible application navigation, not simply small text; this blocks paid knowledge work.
current_workaround: Increase font size, invert contrast, memorize keyboard paths, use a conventional screen reader, or ask a colleague for help.
incumbents_and_gap: NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, and Windows Narrator read exposed accessibility trees, but do not let a user record a task-specific, plain-language route through a partially accessible web workflow.
smallest_useful_product: A Chromium extension that lets a user save 3-10 named steps for a site, announces the current step and its visible anchor, and provides large, high-contrast next/back controls. Non-goals: autonomous clicking, credential handling, or a replacement screen reader.
success_measure: In a 10-user pilot, 7 users complete a saved five-step web workflow without sighted assistance on three separate days.
monetization: one-time — the extension works locally and should remain usable without an account.
constraints: All saved routes stay in browser storage; never inspect password fields; use the accessibility tree before visual heuristics; test with NVDA rather than claiming conformance.
why_distinct: It preserves a person's own reliable workflow through imperfect enterprise software instead of attempting to replace a screen reader with an AI agent.

title: Point & Speak Desktop
user: Low-vision desktop users who encounter remote desktops, legacy software, games, and canvas-heavy interfaces that expose no usable accessibility tree.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker says accessibility APIs fail on unusual workplace software and explicitly asks about a screen-recorder/camera-to-TTS computer-vision approach.
Budgie's open request 'Improve Screen Reader Support' confirms desktop screen-reader coverage remains an active platform gap.

recurrence: Two 2025 desktop-accessibility requests point to the same failure mode: unavailable or incomplete semantic UI data.
current_workaround: Try OCR tools, magnify the whole display, switch platforms, or rely on a sighted helper.
incumbents_and_gap: Narrator, NVDA, Orca, and VoiceOver are strongest where apps publish metadata; generic OCR utilities read a full screen and are slow to control precisely.
smallest_useful_product: A local desktop app with a global hotkey: drag a region, OCR it on-device, and speak, copy, or pin the result at adjustable speed. Non-goals: continuous surveillance, automatic actions, remote streaming, or cloud image upload.
success_measure: At least 70% of pilot captures produce a usable spoken result in under two seconds for 20 representative regions.
monetization: one-time — on-device accessibility software has a strong privacy expectation and no operating cost per capture.
constraints: Use local OCR/TTS; obtain OS screen-capture permission transparently; never retain captures by default; clearly label it as assistive, not a safety or medical product.
why_distinct: The interaction is intentional region selection with predictable local output, not an always-on vision model or a general-purpose image chatbot.

title: Next Physical Step
user: Adults with ADHD who freeze at choosing a task or lose track of an unfinished household action and need one concrete re-entry cue.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker with ADHD says choosing what to do next is the problem; commenters ask for reminders to put things away, flexible lists, and less decision-making.
A 2025 request for enhanced keyboard accessibility is a related reminder that lower-interaction, keyboard-first interfaces matter when attention and motor context are constrained.

recurrence: The ADHD thread contains multiple incompatible wishes for ordinary task apps, but they converge on decision friction and returning to a real-world task.
current_workaround: Maintain elaborate task lists, snooze reminders, use Pomodoro apps, or leave notes that are later ignored.
incumbents_and_gap: Todoist, TickTick, Finch, Habitica, and Structured manage lists and schedules; none makes a deliberately tiny 'what is the next visible physical action?' card the whole product.
smallest_useful_product: An offline PWA with one active card: a 120-character next action, optional photo, location-free return time, and Done/Not now. It hides all backlog until the current card is resolved. Non-goals: diagnosis, scoring, social accountability, calendar replacement, or punitive notifications.
success_measure: In a 21-day opt-in pilot, median active-card completion is at least 50% and fewer than 20% of notifications are disabled.
monetization: free — accessibility utility adoption and trust matter more than extracting payment from a vulnerable group; a paid export could follow only if requested.
constraints: No medical claims; no dark-pattern streaks or shame copy; encrypt optional photo data locally; reminders must be easy to silence.
why_distinct: It rejects the crowded AI-prioritized to-do-list model in favor of a single low-cognitive-load re-entry prompt.

title: Caption Salience
user: People with partial or high-frequency hearing loss who use captions while retaining some audio and need uncertain or acoustically important words to stand out.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker proposes bolding caption words likely to be misheard and asks for hearing-loss-specific caption styling.
The 38-reaction request 'Realtime closed captions generation' shows continuing demand for better real-time caption support.

recurrence: Across a streaming-caption request and a highly reacted real-time-caption issue, captions are treated as a live assistive interface rather than a transcript afterthought.
current_workaround: Turn captions on, repeatedly rewind, increase system volume, or accept that speech and text do not line up with the parts that were hard to hear.
incumbents_and_gap: Live Caption, Ava, Google Meet, Zoom, and OS caption systems render text, but generally offer only global font/background settings rather than a user-controlled salience layer for uncertainty and named speakers.
smallest_useful_product: A local caption-player companion for user-provided WebVTT/SRT or microphone captions that marks low-confidence tokens, speaker changes, and user-defined terms with accessible emphasis presets. Non-goals: extracting captions from DRM services, diagnosing hearing loss, or cloud transcription by default.
success_measure: In captioned comprehension tests, participants flag at least 20% fewer missed key words with their chosen preset than with plain captions.
monetization: one-time — the core is a local rendering aid, with no reason to meter a disability accommodation.
constraints: Use confidence only when supplied by a transcription engine; do not claim accuracy; support screen-reader-safe emphasis; avoid copyrighted video ingestion.
why_distinct: This is a caption presentation control surface, not another speech-to-text service.

title: Caption Style Checker
user: Independent video educators and accessibility reviewers who need to catch caption files that lose speaker cues, emphasis, placement notes, or readability before publication.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The post documents YouTube stripping advanced subtitle features such as styling, positioning, ruby text, and font choices from existing videos.
SmartTube's open feature request is explicitly 'Support enhanced captions.'

recurrence: Two independent video-platform communities request or report loss of enhanced caption semantics in 2025-26.
current_workaround: Hand-inspect caption files, upload a private test video, or settle for the platform's basic caption conversion.
incumbents_and_gap: Subtitle Edit and Aegisub are powerful editors; platform uploaders silently flatten or reject features and offer little preflight feedback aimed at accessibility meaning.
smallest_useful_product: A local drag-and-drop WebVTT/SRT/TTML linter that previews several accessible styles and reports lost semantics, overlong reading speed, missing speaker labels, and unsupported tags per selected platform profile. Non-goals: video hosting, automatic translation, or scraping/uploading platform media.
success_measure: At least 80% of pilot creators fix one preflight warning before publishing, and no supported warning is a false parse error on the supplied fixtures.
monetization: free — a local standards checker benefits from transparent rules and open fixtures; paid batch CI can be considered later.
constraints: Ship parsers under compatible licenses; document that platform support changes; process files in-browser and do not upload subtitles.
why_distinct: It verifies accessibility semantics at the publishing boundary instead of competing as a general subtitle editor.

title: Color Meaning Lens
user: Color-blind people working in dashboards, documents, and code reviews where state is communicated by hue alone.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A technical worker asks how people handle color blindness on screens; a commenter reports missing dark-red text and needing authors not to rely on color.
The issue is titled 'Code diff view is not accessible for people with red-green color blindness.'

recurrence: Two 2026 technical-work examples show the cost is not aesthetic preference: important changes and state can be missed.
current_workaround: Enable an OS color filter, use EnChroma glasses, ask a colleague, or request that authors avoid color-only communication.
incumbents_and_gap: Windows/macOS color filters and browser devtools simulate deficiencies, but they transform every pixel and do not expose the semantic distinction a user is trying to inspect.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension activated with a hotkey that samples repeated color groups in the current page and overlays temporary pattern/letter badges plus contrast warnings. Non-goals: system-wide recoloring, medical color correction, or claims of accurately simulating every condition.
success_measure: In a dashboard-state identification test, users correctly identify 90% of color-only states after enabling the lens, versus their own baseline.
monetization: free — the core should be usable on work pages without a subscription or page data leaving the browser.
constraints: Run only on an explicit hotkey; do not transmit page pixels; avoid modifying input controls; make overlay labels keyboard-accessible.
why_distinct: It adds inspectable, temporary meaning to a live interface rather than applying a blunt global color filter.

title: Speak Page Actions
user: People with limited vision or hand mobility who need to operate ordinary browser pages by speaking a small, reviewable set of visible actions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker wants to say 'click publish' in Firefox; commenters describe stitching Talon, Vimium, or numbered inputs together and flag the offline gap.
VS Code users request line numbers be exposed specifically so Windows 11 Voice Access can navigate them.

recurrence: The older direct end-user request and a still-open 2025 Voice Access integration request show both browser and app semantics are incomplete.
current_workaround: Use Dragon/Talon/Vimium combinations, numbered-link overlays, keyboard shortcuts, or proprietary browser add-ons.
incumbents_and_gap: Windows Voice Access, macOS Voice Control, Dragon, Talon, and Rango are broad systems; their setup, cloud dependence, and inconsistent page semantics leave a niche for a transparent page-scoped command layer.
smallest_useful_product: A Chromium extension that enumerates visible, labelled buttons/links/form fields, supports offline grammar for 'click <label>', then shows a confirmation for destructive actions. Non-goals: voice passwords, banking automation, background microphone capture, or a general assistant.
success_measure: Users successfully invoke 85% of a 20-action public-site test set without looking at numbered overlays.
monetization: one-time — local voice controls are a durable assistive layer, not a metered transcription service.
constraints: Local speech recognition where browser/OS permits; push-to-talk only; never read masked fields; confirmation and undo for submits/deletes; respect site CSP and permissions.
why_distinct: It deliberately narrows voice control to inspectable accessible page actions, avoiding an unreliable, overreaching voice agent.

title: Game Text Beacon
user: Blind and low-vision PC players who need an on-demand way to read a dialogue, menu, or objective from games that lack screen-reader support.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Linux player says no open-source tool let them hear game text, so they built a GPU-accelerated select-to-speak overlay for games and video.
Flutter's open issue reports map markers are not recognized by accessibility tools, a representative example of visual elements bypassing assistive metadata.

recurrence: The 2026 game request and 2025 UI-metadata failure share a clear need for an on-demand fallback when labels are visually rendered only.
current_workaround: Use OCR tools not designed for games, magnify the display, rely on a companion, or skip inaccessible titles.
incumbents_and_gap: NVDA and Windows Narrator need exposed app semantics; community mods are title-specific; generic OCR does not provide a low-friction gamepad-friendly trigger.
smallest_useful_product: A Windows/Linux desktop overlay that takes a user-drawn or gamepad-positioned region on hotkey, reads it locally, and queues speech without intercepting game input. Non-goals: gameplay automation, anti-cheat bypass, multiplayer overlays, or cloud screenshots.
success_measure: In five supported windowed titles, a player retrieves target menu/dialogue text in under three seconds in 80% of attempts.
monetization: free — title compatibility depends on community testing and the utility should be accessible without a paywall.
constraints: Start windowed/borderless only; publish anti-cheat compatibility guidance; local-only screenshots; do not ship game assets or bypass DRM.
why_distinct: Its gamepad-aware, intentional capture model targets unsupported visual text rather than promising full automated game accessibility.

title: Local Caption Tape
user: Deaf, hard-of-hearing, and attention-variable professionals who need an immediately searchable, private transcript of their own meetings without surrendering recordings to a SaaS notetaker.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker wants a background macOS transcription pipeline with local transcription, local diarization, CLI output, and no dependency on a vendor's auth.
The active feature request is simply 'Live Captions,' indicating that desktop-level caption coverage is still requested.

recurrence: Two 2026 requests independently favor continuous captions but expose the missing local, user-controlled workflow.
current_workaround: Use Zoom/Meet captions, a cloud meeting bot, manual notes, or vendor-bound transcript exports.
incumbents_and_gap: Otter, Fireflies, Granola, Zoom, and macOS tools offer transcription; many are cloud-first, meeting-bot-centric, or hard to export into an existing notes workflow.
smallest_useful_product: A local desktop app that captions selected system/microphone audio, keeps a rolling encrypted transcript, and exports timestamped Markdown/TXT when explicitly saved. Non-goals: recording bystanders without consent, automatic meeting joining, cloud summaries, or behavioral analytics.
success_measure: At least 75% of pilot users find a requested spoken phrase from the prior hour in under 15 seconds without sending audio to a server.
monetization: one-time — local processing has a clear ongoing compute cost borne by the user's own device and avoids a surveillance subscription.
constraints: Obtain jurisdiction-appropriate recording consent; default to transcript-only retention with a clear deletion timer; support local models; disclose speaker attribution uncertainty.
why_distinct: The product is a private, ephemeral caption memory rather than an AI meeting-minutes wrapper.

title: Listen Back Reader
user: Dyslexic readers and people with cognitive fatigue who need a source-faithful read-aloud loop for dense web text without losing their place.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The HN post is titled 'Bast Text to Speech Tool,' reflecting continuing interest in practical text-to-speech tooling.
The issue requests a 'read-aloud / replay audio button,' with 11 reactions, for assistant responses.

recurrence: Two 2026 tool communities ask for read-aloud and replay rather than more generated prose, indicating a delivery and retention problem.
current_workaround: Use browser read-aloud, copy text to a TTS app, or repeatedly restart a paragraph after losing place.
incumbents_and_gap: Speechify, NaturalReader, Edge Read Aloud, and OS TTS can read pages, but often lack a minimal per-sentence replay/keybinding loop that stays anchored to the original web source.
smallest_useful_product: A privacy-first browser extension that extracts the selected article, speaks one sentence at a time with replay/slow/skip controls, and follows the sentence with a high-visibility focus marker. Non-goals: text rewriting, dyslexia diagnosis, voice cloning, accounts, or cloud text upload.
success_measure: In a pilot reading task, users resume the correct sentence after a 10-minute interruption in at least 80% of trials.
monetization: free — browser/OS voices make a no-account basic utility viable and accessible to students.
constraints: Honor page permissions and no-copy signals where applicable; use native/local voices; preserve source links; do not market a particular font or TTS as treatment.
why_distinct: It is a source-anchored retention aid, not another generic text-to-speech reader or an LLM simplifier.

title: Haptic Braille Drills
user: Deaf-blind adults and their communication partners who want short, repeatable smartphone haptic drills for learning or retaining a tactile alphabet.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A prototype creator asks about the learning curve for Vibro-Braille on a smartphone touch screen for deaf-blind communication and navigation.
The open issue asks that dyslexia fonts be easier to find, illustrating continuing demand for direct, user-selectable reading accommodations rather than hidden settings.

recurrence: A direct 2025 tactile-communication request plus a 2026 accommodation-discoverability request support a small, explicitly configurable accessibility utility.
current_workaround: Learn with a person, use printed charts, or use inaccessible/general flashcard apps that give visual feedback first.
incumbents_and_gap: Braille education apps and flashcards focus on visual Braille or expensive hardware; a phone's vibration motor can provide a no-extra-hardware practice surface but needs careful, teachable patterns.
smallest_useful_product: An offline Android PWA with configurable vibration patterns, one-symbol listen-and-repeat drills, adjustable pauses, and an optional large-print partner view. Non-goals: emergency navigation, clinical communication claims, automatic translation, or claiming to replace Braille instruction.
success_measure: After five self-guided sessions, at least 60% of opt-in learners correctly identify 10 configured patterns at 80% accuracy in an in-app test.
monetization: free — participatory testing with a small community is more important than gating basic communication practice.
constraints: Co-design and usability-test with deaf-blind users before admission; vibration APIs vary by device; no safety-critical navigation claims; include an immediate stop control.
why_distinct: It is a narrowly testable tactile-practice tool, not a speculative AI guide or a replacement for assistive hardware.

title: Accessible Page Capture
user: Low-vision workers and the colleagues supporting them who need to report one inaccessible web interaction with enough evidence for a product team to fix it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker describes visually impaired people needing real environmental awareness for daily tasks, emphasizing that failures in access have concrete functional impact.
The 23-reaction open issue is titled 'Posthog Does Not Comply with Accessibility Standards.'

recurrence: A 2025 accessibility-compliance issue with substantial reactions and a separate low-vision request show that inaccessible experiences persist even in sophisticated software.
current_workaround: Send an imprecise support email, record a screen video, try to identify ARIA failures in devtools, or wait for an accessibility audit.
incumbents_and_gap: axe DevTools, WAVE, Lighthouse, and enterprise audit platforms diagnose code-level rules; a non-developer needs a compact replayable account of what they attempted and what assistive output was missing.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension that records an explicit 30-second interaction trace, page URL, focused element labels, and optional user note, then exports a redacted Markdown/JSON issue packet. Non-goals: continuous session recording, submitting issues automatically, accessibility certification, or uploading confidential page content.
success_measure: In a pilot with 10 reported barriers, receiving product teams can reproduce at least 8 from the exported packet without a follow-up meeting.
monetization: freemium — an individual local export stays free; a paid team inbox can coordinate consented reports without changing the core utility.
constraints: Explicit start/stop and preview; redact typed values and password fields; no recording by default; ensure the extension itself is keyboard and screen-reader accessible; avoid legal conformance claims.
why_distinct: It converts a lived access barrier into a reproducible engineering artifact rather than adding another automated accessibility scanner.
